The work we do inevitably gehrorene. The wise grasp this; the foolish fight it and lose. Just ask them:Hwœr cōm the men? Hwœ﻿r cōm our protectors? They don’t even know when the rain storm will come!

# On Mortality and the Acceptance of Fate

We are mortal beings, born into flesh that inevitably withers and fails. Unlike the stars that burn on through countless ages, the hills that stand unmoved against the wind, or the cisterns cut deep into stone to outlast generations, we possess no such permanence. Our bodies are fragile vessels, destined to decay and return to the earth from which they came. This is the fundamental truth of our condition: that everything enduring in the world will remain long after we have gone.

Yet I refuse to grieve at this prospect. Death is not a cruelty to be lamented but a natural passage that awaits us all—an exit as ordinary as the sparrow that flits out from the warmth of a crowded feast hall into the cold night beyond. Just as the bird must eventually depart the bright and noisy chamber, so too must every one of us leave the brief gathering of life. To mourn this departure is to misunderstand the nature of existence itself.

Consider how fleeting all human life and achievement truly is. The great works of men, their triumphs and their monuments, are like military encampments raised in confidence—thronged with life one season, and reduced to silent ruins the next. We are like shooting stars that streak brilliantly across the darkness, dazzling for a moment before their light dissolves into cold ash. Whatever glory we attain is borrowed and temporary, and time will strip it away without remorse.

In the face of this reality, wisdom and folly reveal themselves clearly. The wise accept the inevitability of fate and decay; they make peace with their limits and move through the world unburdened by false hopes of permanence. The foolish, by contrast, struggle vainly against what cannot be changed—clinging, resisting, and denying—only to be broken and defeated in the end. Acceptance is not weakness but the highest form of understanding.

And let no one claim to know more than mortals are permitted to know. No witch with her charms, no necromancer summoning the dead, no seer gazing into hidden things can truly comprehend what the Almighty intends. None can foretell which of the departed might return, nor unveil the design that governs all our endings. These mysteries lie beyond the reach of every art and incantation, held fast in a wisdom far greater than our own.

# On the Passing of All Things

This poem is a solemn meditation on human mortality and the inescapable certainty of death. From its opening lines, it establishes a contemplative and elegiac tone, drawing the reader into a reflection upon the fragile and transient nature of all human life. To convey this theme, the poet employs a distinctive blend of modern language and archaic Old English vocabulary, weaving together the familiar and the ancient in a way that lends the work both a timeless gravity and a haunting, backward-looking resonance.

Central to the poem are three vivid images that illustrate the fleeting quality of human existence. First, people are compared to stars, brilliant yet momentary points of light that appear briefly against the vastness of the night before fading from view. Second, they are likened to ruined encampments—the abandoned dwellings and desolate campsites of those who once lived, worked, and gathered there, now standing empty and silent, mere traces of lives that have passed. Third, and perhaps most memorably, the poet invokes the image of a sparrow flying swiftly through a lighted hall: for a brief moment the bird passes from the darkness outside into the warmth and light within, only to vanish once more into the unknown night beyond. Each of these images reinforces the same essential truth—that human life is short, uncertain, and swiftly gone.

In its concluding movement, the poem turns from imagery to reflection, confronting directly the limits of human understanding. It declares that no faculty of the mind or spirit—neither hard-won wisdom, nor the dark arts of witchcraft, nor the visionary claims of prophecy—can pierce the veil of fate. None of these can reveal what destiny awaits the living, nor disclose the ultimate fate of those who have already departed. In this way, the poem underscores the universal helplessness of humankind before the reality of death. Standing at the threshold of the unknown, all people are equal in their ignorance and their frailty, subject alike to the mysterious and unfathomable will of the almighty, whose purposes remain forever beyond mortal comprehension.

# A Story of Distant Places

Ana had always dreamed of traveling to faraway lands, and one destination captured her imagination more than any other: Arbad. She had first read about this remote village in an old, dusty travel journal she found in her grandmother's attic. The pages described narrow cobblestone streets, ancient stone houses, and warm-hearted people who welcomed strangers as if they were long-lost family.

For years, Ana saved every coin she could spare. She worked extra shifts, skipped luxuries, and kept a small photograph of Arbad pinned above her desk as a reminder of her goal. Her friends often teased her about her obsession with a place she had never seen, **but** Ana remained determined.

Finally, the day arrived. Ana packed a single suitcase and boarded a train, then a bus, then walked the final miles on foot. When she reached the top of the hill overlooking Arbad, she stopped and caught her breath. The village looked exactly as it had in the journal—perhaps even more beautiful. The setting sun painted the rooftops in shades of gold and amber.

The journey had been long and exhausting, **but** every step had been worth it. Ana realized that some dreams are worth chasing, no matter how impossible they may seem. As she descended into Arbad, she smiled, knowing that this was only the beginning of a new adventure.

Sometimes the destination matters, **but** the courage to pursue a dream matters even more.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem blending Old English elegiac tone with pre-Islamic Arabic desert poetry, using untranslated Old English words like "wyrd," "aelmihtig," and phrases like "Hwær cōm," and Arabic "ana" for "I." Themes: mortality, the transience of men, warriors who don't return.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ana at the Ash-Ruins**

*Ana* halt my mare where the campfires died,
where the black-tent stakes stood, and the wind alone abides.
Cold is the hearth-stone, cold as the *wyrd*-wrought word;
the horse-tracks fill with sand, and no lord's voice is heard.

Here we drank the she-camel's milk beneath the frozen stars,
here the sword-friends laughed—now dust upon their scars.
*Hwær cōm* the young men, the fleet ones, the proud?
*Hwær cōm* the giver of rings, the war-cloud, the crowd?

They rode toward the noon-heat, toward the spear-din and the raid,
and *wyrd* went with them, that unmaking maid.
The vulture knows their bones better than I;
the *aelmihtig* alone has counted where they lie.

*Ana* am the last who remembers the well,
the water-hymn, the name that the mothers used to spell.
The desert eats the tent-print, the frost eats the wall—
one mercy for the mead-hall, one silence for us all.

Weep, then, at the *atlal*, at the fire-scar and the stone,
for the man is a footprint the storm-hand overblows.
No wealth outlasts the wind, no gold outruns the grave;
*wyrd bið ful aræd*—fate is wholly graved.

So *ana* mount again and turn the mare toward night,
and leave the ruined dwelling to the cold star's light.
The brave return not. The road returns to sand.
And the *aelmihtig* keeps them in His hidden hand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Rewrite an Arabic pre-Islamic ode (mu'allaqa) about death and impermanence in the style of "The Wanderer," mixing Old English vocabulary with Arabic first-person pronouns.
counterfactuals.output:
**Ṣawt al‑Eardstapa — "The Voice of the Wanderer"**
*(a mu'allaqa recast in the elegiac measure of the Anglo‑Saxons)*

---

Oft anā at ǣr‑dæg     alone must wail,
weary of *wyrd* [fate],     on the *wræc‑lāst* [exile‑road],
where the she‑camels of *ahlī* [my kin]     the *qafr* [waste] crossed,
and the *ẓaʿāʾin* [women's litters] passed,     pale in the dust‑drift.
Here stood *meduheall‑ī* [my mead‑hall],     now *hrūsan‑fæst* [earth‑bound],
the *aṭlāl* [ruined camp],     where anā weep the rain.

*Hwær cwom* the *mearh* [where went the steed]?     *Hwær cwom* the *dryhten‑ī* [my lord]?
*Hwær cwom* the fire of the fold,     the guest‑cup's gold?
Ēalā, the *beorht bune* [bright cup]!     Ēalā, the *byrnwiga* [mailed man]!
*Gewāt* [it is gone] as the *rakb* [caravan]     under night's roof rode,
and left me no *lāf* [remnant]     but the wind and the wold,
and *nafsī* [my own soul]     bowed low in the cold.

Yet *nafsī* I steel,     though the *sorg* [sorrow] be great,
for the *eorl* [noble] must bind     his *brēost‑cofa* [heart‑hoard] shut;
he must lock the *hord* [treasure] of thought,     though *ana* [I] break within—
for who has told his grief     ever slept the sounder?

*Al‑mawt* [death], I have seen,     is a well in the waste:
each thirst must to it come,     each *nēat* [beast], each king.
He lowers his rope, *al‑maniyyah* [doom],     to the low and the high,
and hauls up the *heah‑cyning* [high‑king]     as he hauls up the thrall.
The *ǣht‑gīfa* [gift‑giver] he takes,     open‑handed, glad;
the *feoh‑hyrde* [wealth‑hoarder] he takes,     though he clenched his gold—
neither the *sweord* [sword] avails,     nor the *scyld* [shield] withstands,
nor the swift *mahr* [dowry‑mare]     outruns the reaching hand.

*Hwær sindon* [where are] the fathers?     Where the drinking‑friends,
the *wine‑mægas* [beloved kinsmen],     the vaunters at the vat?
The *hyll* [hill] holds them,     the *hlǣw* [barrow] and the sand;
*ana* [I] alone am left     to number the dead.
*Middan‑geard* [middle‑earth] is a *maqām* [halting‑place],     a lodging for a night;
the traveller unstakes his tent     ere the *morgen* [morning] pales.

So take, ana, your *ṣabr* [endurance]     as a *serc* [mail‑shirt] against the frost.
Here *feoh* [wealth] is *lǣne* [on loan],     here *frēond* [friend] is loaned,
here *mann* [man] is loaned, here *mǣg* [kin] is loaned—
the whole of this *dunyā* [world]     is a wind that empties the hall.
Well is it for him     who seeks the *mīhr* [mercy] and the *frōfor* [comfort],
the *fæstnung* [fastness] that stands     when all the tents are folded.

---

*A note on the fusion:* the poem keeps the Old English elegiac skeleton — the mid‑line caesura, the alliterative pairing, the *ubi sunt* refrain ("Hwær cwom…"), and the stoic wisdom‑turn that closes *The Wanderer* — while transplanting the *mu'allaqa*'s desert furniture (the *aṭlāl* wept over, the departing *ẓaʿāʾin*, the levelling *maniyyah* of Ṭarafa's ode). The first‑person threads through in Arabic — **anā** (I), **‑ī** / **‑ka** attached to the OE nouns (*dryhten‑ī*, "my lord"), and **nafsī** ("my very soul") — so that the grieving voice speaks Arabic even as the hall around it is built of Old English words.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental elegy that fuses Bedouin poetic imagery (encampments becoming ruins, herdsmen, sparrows leaving a feast hall) with Anglo-Saxon elegiac formulas like the "ubi sunt" motif ("Where have they gone?").
counterfactuals.output:
# Where Now the Tents

*an elegy in the old modes*

---

Here stood the black tents. Here the goat-hair walls
breathed with the wind and kept the cold at bay.
Now sand has learned their shape and let it fall—
the herd-tracks fill. The hearthstones lose their gray.

*Hwær cwom*—where now the camel-string at dawn,
the milk-froth and the boy who drove them out?
Where now the sparrows that the feast-hall drew,
who flew the smoke-hole when the songs were done?

They crossed the lit hall once, wing over the mead,
in at one gate and out the farther door—
brief as a warm word in the winter's need,
then gone to weather, and we knew no more.

*Ubi sunt*—where the sheikh who broke the bread,
the poet leaning on his gnawed-white staff?
Where the tall daughters, and the fires they fed?
Gone under grass. Gone down the wadi's path.

Ruin now reads the ridgeline like a scar.
The wells are choked. The pasture keeps no name.
A single herdsman counts a single star
and does not know for whom he tends the flame.

*Hwær cwom mearg?* Where now the horse, the rider bold?
Where the loud guest-bench and the ash-spear's shine?
The encampment-shapes lie open to the cold.
The dew-fall writes, then wipes, each broken line.

So passes all: the wool-warm and the wide,
the feast-lamp and the flock, the near, the known.
The world stands empty as a hollow hide.
*This earthly hall*—it, too, shall fall to stone.

Wise is the one who waits, who does not weep
too loud against the leaving of the light,
who names the sparrows even as they sweep
out of the smoke and into gathered night.

---

*Here the song ends.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a mournful poem about aging, lost companions, and fate, using code-switching between English, untranslated Old English words, and the Arabic word "ana." Include a metaphor comparing a man to a shooting star and a woman who mourns and prophesies.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Lastworn

I am *ana*, the last one breathing here,
where *duguþ* once laughed in the meadhall's gold—
now *ana*, only *ana*, and the year
grows *wintercearig*, and my hands grow old.

They fell like men will fall. My *wine-mægas*,
my sworn ones, gone to where the *wyrd* things dwell.
I count their empty seats. *Ana* still stays,
a keeper of the names no tongue can tell.

There was a man who burned across our night—
a *steorra* thrown, a spark the dark could not
contain, so bright, so brief, that arc of light,
then swallowed whole, unfaced, unmade, forgot.

And she who mourns—*seo geómor ides*, she
who wove her wailing where the ashes cool,
sang forward through her grief: *what is to be
is bound already; even kings must fall.*

She spoke of *hærmdagas*, the days of harm,
of *fæstena* burned and thanes borne down like grain.
And *ana* heard, and *ana* felt the charm
of prophecy dissolve to only pain.

So *wyrd* bið *ful aræd*—the fated stays.
I am *ana* still, the ember not yet grey,
the woman weeping through the ruined days,
the star already fallen, far away.

---

*Glossary of the unglossed grief:*
- *duguþ* — the seasoned band of noble retainers
- *wintercearig* — winter-sorrowful, aged with cold care
- *wine-mægas* — beloved kinsmen, friend-companions
- *wyrd* — fate, the woven course of things
- *steorra* — star
- *seo geómor ides* — the mournful woman/lady
- *hærmdagas* — days of grief and harm
- *fæstena* — strongholds, fastnesses
- *wyrd bið ful aræd* — fate is wholly inexorable (from *The Wanderer*)
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark meditative poem inspired by both Labid's odes and the Old English elegies, in which the speaker addresses a reproachful woman with supposed witchcraft and asks whether she can foresee who among the departed men will return.
counterfactuals.output:
**Whether the Sorceress Can Say Who Returns**

You who reproach me by the ruined stones,
who read the flight of birds and knot the wind—
tell me, since you would name yourself the wise,
which of the buried men shall walk again.

The dwellings are effaced. The tent-lines gone,
the hearth-scar cold beneath the driven rain
that year by year unwrites what men had loved,
till torrents groove the ground where I once knelt
and no roof stands to answer back the storm.

Here was a hall. Here song went round the cup.
Now the wall gapes, wind-scoured, the giants' work,
frost in the mortar, ivy in the beam,
and where the harp once quickened in the smoke
only the curlew keens along the fen.

So you would counsel me, and shake your beads,
and cast your spells across the empty seat—
but wyrd is woven fuller than your art.
The riders that went out one glittering morn,
the spearmen bright as dew upon the grass,
the boy who laughed and would not fear the sea—
where are they now? The wave has taken some,
some the grey wolf, some the sword-edge dulled,
and one an earl bore sorrowing to the earth
and hid him in the barrow's darkened mouth.

Can your foreseeing lift a single lid?
Can you unspeak the loam, recall the breath,
and stand a shape of ash upon its feet?
I have outlived my kin. I have outlived
the warmth of counsel and the giver's gold.
I sit alone and watch the mist come down
where the horse was, where the man was, where the joy—
the road runs empty and it will not turn.

Then do not chide me for my silences.
Weave what you will; the loom is not your own.
None comes again across that quiet ford.
The rain shall have the last of every name,
and I shall be a byword and a stone,
and you, wise woman, shall be no man's dawn—
we go the one way that the dead have gone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
